front: TC013: What is the minimum viable move?
back: Name one piece of effort you noticed today that would normally go unacknowledged. Say it without qualifying it or immediately moving on.

front: TC013: What is the core sequence?
back: Notice the specific work -> Name it aloud -> Do not qualify.

front: TC013: What is the field tip?
back: Acknowledge before you ask for the next thing.

front: TC013: What is the strong version of: Moving straight to the next task without acknowledgement?
back: I know how much work went into that. I did not want to move past it without saying so.

front: TC013: What is the strong version of: Generic praise: 'You worked so hard!'?
back: The preparation you put into that presentation was clear — especially under that timeline.

front: TC013: What is the strong version of: Backhanded acknowledgement: 'Finally got there!'?
back: Clean acknowledgement of the effort, no qualifiers.

front: TC013: What is better than: 'Great effort — so, next steps...'?
back: Let the acknowledgement be its own sentence, with air after it, before any next thing.

front: TC013: What is better than: 'You worked really hard on this, but...'?
back: 'You worked really hard on this.' Full stop. The feedback gets its own conversation.

front: TC013: What is better than: 'Well, at least you tried really hard!'?
back: Name the effort honestly and address the result separately — one does not cancel the other.

front: TC013: What are signs it is working?
back: People seem surprised — in a good way — that you noticed. Morale and motivation visibly improve. Trust builds faster than usual. The work continues at the same level or improves.

front: TC013: When should you avoid this technique?
back: When the effort was poor and naming it implies the outcome is acceptable. When managing underperformance — naming effort can inadvertently reward the wrong behaviour.

front: TC013: What is the best recovery line?
back: 'I have noticed your work for months and said none of it out loud. That changes now.'
